summary: Defines a mechanism for an access network to give identity selection hints to an EAP peer so it can pick an appropriate Network Access Identifier. It is useful when the peer does not know which network it is joining or has no direct roaming relationship. It is limited in scalability and suited to a small to moderate number of roaming partners. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a device joins a wireless network, it has to say who it is. If it holds several usernames and cannot tell which network it is joining, it may pick the wrong one. RFC 4284 lets the network answer that question first: the network sends the device a list of the networks it can reach, and the device uses that list to choose.

questions: how do eap devices pick a username
subtitle: A way for the network to tell a wireless device which username it should use when the device cannot tell on its own.

tldr.problem: An EAP client may hold several credentials and cannot tell which network it is joining, or which of several roaming brokers can reach its home network, so it cannot decide which Network Access Identifier to send.
tldr.mechanism: The access network appends an identity hint to the EAP-Request/Identity message, after the displayable text and a NUL character, listing the realms it can reach. A RADIUS proxy that cannot route a request replies with a challenge carrying the hint instead of rejecting the request.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document, developed by 3GPP and verified by the IETF EAP working group as compatible with EAP. Its reach is limited by the EAP MTU, which caps the number of roaming partners that can be advertised.

facts.label: EAP MTU used in the scaling example

today: RFC 4284 is an Informational document from January 2006 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records a mechanism developed by 3GPP; the IESG note states that the EAP working group verified the specification is compatible with EAP as defined in RFC 3748, and that the required 3GPP client behaviour is described in 3GPP TS 24.234.

sections.title: Which Identity Should a Device Use?
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is defined in RFC 3748. An EAP peer, the end of the link that responds to the authenticator, may hold several credentials. Where the lower layer does not indicate which network it is connecting to, or where its home network has roaming relationships with several mediating networks, the peer may be uncertain which Network Access Identifier (NAI) to include in an EAP-Response/Identity.

This document defines a mechanism that lets the access network give the peer identity selection hints, including information about its roaming relationships. The hint is sent in an EAP-Request/Identity message, appended after the displayable message and a NUL character. It may help the peer select a credential and the matching NAI, or format the NAI, as described in RFC 4282, so that the Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) messages reach the right home server. If several mediating networks are available, the peer can influence which one is used.

How the peer actually selects is a matter of its own local policy and configuration, and is outside the scope of this document. The peer could use a different identity, switch to another access network, or reformat its NAI to assist AAA routing. The exact client behaviour is described by the standards bodies using this specification, such as 3GPP TS 24.234. The mechanism was developed by 3GPP, and the IESG note records that the EAP working group verified it is compatible with EAP as defined in RFC 3748.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can hold several usernames, and when it joins a network it may not know which one that network expects. The network can help by sending a list of the networks it can reach before the device has to answer.

sections.title: How Many Hints Fit in One Message
sections.content:
The number of hints that can be provided is limited by the EAP MTU. Assuming 20 octets per hint and an EAP MTU of 1096, a maximum of 50 roaming partners can be advertised. The scaling limits this imposes should be taken into account when deploying the solution.

There is a second limit. Because the mechanism relies on information carried in the EAP-Request/Identity packet, the peer has to choose a point of attachment before it can obtain identity hints. Where several points of attachment are available, the mechanism does not let the peer use the hints in deciding which one to pick. In roaming situations this can mean the peer has to try several points of attachment before it finds a compatible one, which increases handoff latency.

The document relates this to the general network discovery and selection problem, and notes that it solves only a part of that problem. IEEE 802.11 is also looking into more comprehensive and long-term solutions for network discovery and selection.
sections.plainLanguage: Only so many roaming partners fit in one message, and the device has to pick a network before it receives the hint. So the hint helps with the username, not with the choice of network.

sections.title: How the Hint Is Written
sections.content:
The identity hint information is placed after the displayable string and a NUL character in the EAP-Request/Identity. The attribute's value consists of a set of realm names separated by a semicolon, and the ABNF below defines it.

The Network-Info field can contain an NAIRealms list in addition to proprietary information, and the proprietary information can be placed before or after the NAIRealms list. To extract the list, an implementation can either find the NAIRealms= immediately after the NUL character, or seek forward to find ,NAIRealms somewhere in the string. The realms data ends either at the first comma or at the end of the string, whichever comes first.

The RFC gives a sample hex dump of an EAP-Request/Identity packet. The identity part reads Hello!, followed by the NUL character, followed by NAIRealms=example.com;mnc014.mcc310.3gppnetwork.org.
sections.plainLanguage: The hint is a list of domain names separated by semicolons, placed after a NUL character at the end of the identity text. Other information can sit on either side of the list, so a reader looks for the NAIRealms marker rather than assuming where the list starts.

sections.title: How the Hint Changes Proxy Behaviour
sections.content:
The EAP authenticator MAY send an identity hint to the peer in the initial EAP-Request/Identity. If the hint is not sent, for instance because the authenticator does not support this specification, the peer may select the wrong NAI. If the local AAA proxy has no default route configured, it may find that the User-Name(1) attribute in the request contains a realm for which there is no corresponding route.

Where no route is found, existing AAA proxies will typically send an Access-Reject. However, where the request contains an EAP-Message attribute, an AAA proxy implementing this specification should instead reply with a challenge that includes an identity hint. For example, a RADIUS proxy that receives an Access-Request with an EAP-Message attribute and a User-Name(1) attribute containing an unknown realm SHOULD reply with an Access-Challenge carrying an EAP-Message attribute that encapsulates an EAP-Request/Identity packet containing an identity hint, rather than an Access-Reject.

If the peer then responds with an EAP-Response/Identity that still contains an unknown realm, a local AAA proxy or server implementing this specification MUST eventually send an Access-Reject containing an EAP-Failure. Before doing so, it MAY send an Access-Challenge containing an EAP-Notification, to explain the failure. The State(24) attribute of RFC 2865 can be used to determine whether an identity hint had already been sent.

EAP does not support fragmentation of EAP-Request/Identity messages, and the minimum EAP MTU size is 1020 octets, so the maximum length of the identity hint information is limited by the link MTU.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of turning a request away when it does not recognise the realm in the username, the server asks for the identity again and includes a list of the realms it can reach. If the device still picks one the server cannot route, the server then rejects the request.

sections.title: Three Ways to Deliver the Hint
sections.content:
The appendix describes delivery options for IEEE 802.11 access networks, which also apply to other access networks that use EAP for authentication and the NAI format for identifying users. The options assume RADIUS as the AAA protocol, but Diameter could be used instead without significant architectural differences. The main difference between the options is which entity in the access network creates the EAP-Request/Identity.

Option 1 has the access point send the initial EAP-Request/Identity with the hint included, which is the simplest case but needs the mechanism in every access point, and configuring the hint in a potentially large number of access points is problematic if the information changes often. Current access points do not support the mechanism.

Option 2 has the local RADIUS proxy or server create the initial EAP-Request/Identity. Once the peer associates with the access network, the access point sends an EAP-Start message inside a RADIUS Access-Request, and the access network RADIUS server answers with an Access-Challenge carrying the EAP-Request/Identity with the hint. This option can work with current access points as long as they support the EAP-Start message.

Option 3 has the access point send the initial EAP-Request/Identity with no hint. The peer responds, and the response is forwarded to the local RADIUS proxy or server. If the proxy cannot route the message on the identity the peer gave, it sends a second EAP-Request/Identity containing the hint. This option does not require changes to existing network access servers, so it may be preferable in many environments.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three places the hint can come from: the wireless access point, the local authentication server when the device joins, or the local authentication server after it has failed to route the first attempt. The last one needs no changes to existing equipment.

sections.title: Why the Hint Cannot Be Trusted
sections.content:
Identity hint information is delivered inside an EAP-Request/Identity before the authentication conversation begins, so an attacker can modify it. The NAIRealms attribute must therefore be treated as a hint by the peer, that is, as an unreliable indication.

Unauthenticated hints may cause peers to reveal additional identities inadvertently, compromising privacy. Since the EAP-Response/Identity is sent in the clear, this vulnerability already exists; it can be addressed through method-specific identity exchanges. In the same way, where the peer has several identities to choose from, an attacker can use a forged hint to convince the peer to choose an identity bound to a weak EAP method. Requiring the use of strong EAP methods protects against this. A similar issue already exists with respect to unprotected link-layer advertisements such as 802.11 SSIDs.

If the hint is used to select a mediating network, existing EAP methods may not give the home AAA server a way to verify that the mediating network the peer selected was actually the one used. Finally, any information revealed from either the network or the client side before authentication has occurred can be seen as a security risk, because revealing that a network using a weak authentication method is reachable makes it easier for attackers to find it. The consent of the network being advertised in the hints is therefore required before such hints can be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The hint arrives before the device has proved who it is, so anyone on the path could change it. A device must treat it as a suggestion only, use strong authentication methods, and be willing to reveal that it has several identities at all.

viz.caption: OPTION 3: THE HINT ARRIVES AFTER THE FIRST ATTEMPT FAILS

messages.label: Access-Reject
messages.note: Carries EAP-Failure when the realm is still unknown.

viz.caption: THE ABNF FOR AN EAP-REQUEST/IDENTITY CARRYING A HINT

data.title: identity-request-data
data.code:
identity-request-data = [ displayable-string ] %x00 [ Network-Info ]

displayable-string    = *CHAR

Network-Info     =   "NAIRealms=" realm-list
Network-Info     =/  1*OCTET ",NAIRealms=" realm-list
Network-Info     =/  "NAIRealms=" realm-list "," 1*OCTET
Network-Info     =/  1*OCTET ",NAIRealms=" realm-list "," 1*OCTET

realm-list            = realm /
                           ( realm-list ";" realm )

viz.caption: THE THREE DELIVERY OPTIONS IN THE APPENDIX

items.title: Option 1: the access point
items.text: The access point sends the first EAP-Request/Identity and the hint goes in it. Current access points do not support this, and the hint would have to be configured in many of them.

items.title: Option 2: the local RADIUS server at join time
items.text: The access point sends EAP-Start inside an Access-Request and the local RADIUS server answers with an Access-Challenge carrying the hint. It works with current access points that support EAP-Start.

items.title: Option 3: the local RADIUS server after a failure
items.text: The first request goes out with no hint. If the proxy cannot route the reply it sends a second EAP-Request/Identity with the hint. This needs no change to existing network access servers.
